Abbu: Chacha says you haven't been to Friday prayers at the masjid near your college in two months
Irfan: yes. that's true
Abbu: he asked me in front of everyone at the wedding. I didn't know what to say
Abbu: are you in some bad company? is it that Abhinav boy?
Irfan: Abbu, no. Abhinav doesn't even talk about religion. it's me. I've got questions I can't answer yet
Abbu: questions like what
Irfan: are you going to shout?
Abbu: no. I am scared, I won't lie. but I'd rather know you than lose you
Abbu: tell me one question. just one
Irfan: why would God need us to pray at fixed times?
Abbu: good question. my father asked the same one. call me tonight, we'll talk

qa.q: Where did Chacha ask Abbu about Irfan?
qa.a: Chacha asked him in front of everyone at the wedding.

qa.q: Why does Irfan ask 'are you going to shout?'
qa.a: Irfan is nervous, expecting anger and unsure whether it is safe to share his doubts with Abbu.

qa.q: What turning point does Abbu choose, and why does it help?
qa.a: He drops the 'bad company' blame and asks for just one question with curiosity, which keeps Irfan talking whichever way his belief goes.

qa.q: How does the wedding moment affect Abbu?
qa.a: Being asked in front of everyone left Abbu ashamed and lost for words, which is partly why he first reached for blame.

grounding: It shows a father hurt, afraid and embarrassed before relatives by his son's change, then choosing curious listening that protects their bond.

passage:
On the morning of the Varalakshmi puja, Ishita arranged the kalasha in the front room of their house in Hassan and waited. Aditi, home from college in Mysuru, came down in jeans with a book.
'You're not getting ready?'
'I'll help cook, Amma. I don't want to do the puja this year.'
Ishita's hands stopped on the mango leaves. Her sister-in-law would arrive at ten. What would she say? And under that, a colder thought: had she failed her daughter somewhere?
She almost snapped. Instead she wiped her hands, sat on the step and said, 'Tell me what's changed. I'm not angry. I want to understand.'
Aditi sat beside her, surprised. They talked for twenty minutes about books, a friend's funeral, questions with no easy answers. Then Aditi grated coconut, and Ishita lit the lamp alone, with less heaviness than she had expected.

qa.q: Where had Aditi come home from?
qa.a: Aditi had come home from college in Mysuru.

qa.q: What worries went through Ishita's mind when Aditi said no to the puja?
qa.a: She worried what her sister-in-law would say, and feared she had failed her daughter somewhere.

qa.q: Why did Ishita's choice to sit down and ask help?
qa.a: Asking with curiosity instead of snapping kept Aditi talking about her books and questions, protecting their closeness whatever Aditi comes to believe.

qa.q: What would have changed if Ishita had snapped at Aditi?
qa.a: Aditi would likely have gone quiet and kept her questions to herself, and the distance between them could have grown along with the doubts.

grounding: It shows a mother hurt and anxious about relatives when her daughter steps back from a ritual, choosing to listen with curiosity instead of alarm.

passage:
When Mridul came home to Varanasi for the Diwali break, his father, Tushar, noticed it on the first morning: his son didn't join the family at the puja. He stood in the doorway, arms folded, then went back to his phone.
At dinner Tushar's sister asked loudly why Mridul hadn't touched the prasad. Tushar felt his face burn. He imagined the whole family whispering that he had lost his son to the city.
That night he lay awake, hurt and scared. What if Mridul drifted away from everything, from them too?
The next evening, instead of the lecture he had rehearsed, Tushar took Mridul for a walk to the ghats. "You've been reading a lot, I think. Tell me what you're thinking about these days. I'm not going to argue. I want to understand."
Mridul looked at him warily. Then, slowly, he began to talk. They sat on the steps until the evening aarti ended, the father listening more than he ever had.

qa.q: Where did Tushar take Mridul the next evening?
qa.a: For a walk to the ghats.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling at dinner when his sister asked about the prasad?
qa.a: He felt ashamed before the family and hurt, his face burning, afraid of losing his son.

qa.q: Why does Tushar's walk work better than the rehearsed lecture?
qa.a: Listening with curiosity rather than alarm keeps Mridul talking and protects the relationship, whichever way his belief goes.

qa.q: What might Mridul feel when his father asks to understand?
qa.a: Mridul likely feels wary at first, then relieved to be heard instead of judged.

grounding: A father feels hurt, afraid and ashamed before relatives as his son steps back from family practice, then chooses curious listening.

"You didn't sit for the Satyanarayan puja today," Indu said, rolling rotis harder than necessary.
"I was in my room, Amma."
"Your Mama asked where you were. I said you had a headache." She paused. "I felt so small saying that."
"I didn't ask you to lie."
"I know." She put the rolling pin down. "Have you... stopped believing?"
"I don't know. Maybe. I've been reading a lot. I have questions nobody at home ever let me ask."
Indu felt fear rise in her throat. She wanted to say, "Don't talk like that." Instead she asked, "What kind of questions?"
Chinmay looked surprised. "You actually want to know?"
"I'm scared," she admitted. "But I'd rather be scared and know my son than be calm and lose you."
Chinmay pulled up a stool. "Okay. Can I roll the next roti while I explain?"

qa.q: What puja did Chinmay not sit for?
qa.a: The Satyanarayan puja.

qa.q: What did Indu feel when she told Mama about the headache?
qa.a: She felt small and ashamed before the relative, and hurt by her son's absence.

qa.q: What choice by Indu protects the relationship?
qa.a: Instead of saying 'Don't talk like that', she asks with curiosity what his questions are, even while scared.

qa.q: What might Chinmay feel when his mother asks 'What kind of questions?'
qa.a: Chinmay feels surprised and relieved, finally allowed to share what he has been thinking.

grounding: A mother feels shame before relatives and fear for her son's changing belief, but chooses to listen with curiosity.

passage:
When my son Arun came home from college last year and said he no longer went to church, my first feeling was fear. Then shame. What would Father Thomas say? What would my sisters say at Christmas?
I cried in the bathroom that night. I prayed he would come back to his senses.
It was my colleague Pema, a Buddhist, who changed how I saw it. Over lunch she said, "When my daughter questioned everything, I decided to be curious instead of frightened. Otherwise I'd have lost her, not just her beliefs."
So the next time Arun visited, I didn't lecture. I asked what he'd been reading and what he found beautiful. He talked for two hours about philosophers I'd never heard of. I didn't agree with everything. But I learned more about my son that evening than in the whole year before.
I'm Gopika. I still pray for him. And now he tells me things.

qa.q: What did Pema say she decided to be?
qa.a: Curious instead of frightened.

qa.q: What did Gopika feel when Arun said he no longer went to church?
qa.a: Gopika felt fear first, then shame about what the priest and relatives would think.

qa.q: What did Gopika change, and why did it help?
qa.a: Asking Arun what he read and found beautiful instead of lecturing, which kept him talking and protected their bond.

qa.q: How might Arun have experienced that evening?
qa.a: Arun likely felt respected and relieved, able to share his thinking without being lectured.

grounding: A parent feels fear and shame when a son stops going to church, then learns to listen with curiosity, protecting the relationship.

passage:
Note from Kalyani, Lokesh's mother, written for myself after Diwali
Lokesh came home from his hostel for the holidays and did not come to the Lakshmi puja. He sat in his room with a book. When his Mama asked where he was, I said he had a headache. I was ashamed, lying like that in front of my brother. Later I cried in the kitchen. I was afraid: had someone at college turned him against us? Had we failed him?
The next morning I nearly started shouting. Instead I made his favourite poha and asked him what he was reading. He looked surprised. It was a book about the history of religions. He talked for almost an hour, about questions he'd had since Class 11. I didn't agree with everything. But I listened, and I asked more.
What I will do next: keep asking. He is still my son, whatever he decides.

qa.q: What did Kalyani tell Lokesh's Mama when he asked where Lokesh was?
qa.a: She said he had a headache.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel when Lokesh skipped the Lakshmi puja?
qa.a: Kalyani felt ashamed in front of her brother and afraid that college had turned Lokesh against the family, and she cried in the kitchen.

qa.q: What choice protected the relationship, and why?
qa.a: Kalyani chose to make poha and ask with curiosity what Lokesh was reading instead of shouting, which let him talk openly and kept the bond safe whatever he decides.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt when his mother asked about his book?
qa.a: Lokesh was probably surprised and relieved to be asked instead of scolded, which is why he talked for almost an hour.

grounding: Shows a parent hurt, afraid and ashamed before a relative when a grown child steps back from ritual, then choosing to listen with curiosity instead of alarm.
